title: How do you model transaction costs in your backtests? Feels like everyone underestimates it
author: socialwhizca
selftext:
Seeing a lot of "my bot is profitable in backtest" posts and I suspect a chunk of them die live purely because the cost model was too optimistic, assuming a tiny fixed spread and zero slippage that doesn't survive real fills.



How do you handle it? I run on a fixed-spread broker (AvaTrade) mostly because it makes the cost side a constant instead of a guess, so backtest and live costs line up better, though slippage on the actual fill is still its own beast. Curious whether the raw/ECN crowd models variable spread + commission separately or just slaps a flat number on it.



What's your transaction-cost assumption, and how close did live end up vs backtest once costs were real?

comments.author: ibrahim_40
comments.body: A flat spread alone is usually too optimistic. I'd model spread, commissions (if applicable), a slippage buffer based on volatility or news and occasional partial fills. Then I'd compare live vs backtest over a few weeks and keep adjusting until the assumptions consistently match reality

comments.author: tradematesHQ
comments.body:
Transaction costs are definitely the silent killer of many backtests. The problem is that even a "good" flat spread assumption can fall apart when you factor in slippage from order size relative to volume or sudden volatility spikes. If you're using Claude or a chatbot to code your strategy, it's easy to get a clean backtest that looks profitable because the cost model is too simple—but that doesn't mean the stock selection itself is sound.

Before you even get to modeling costs, you need to know which stocks are worth backtesting. That's where trademates.co comes in as a better first step: it gives you structured stock analysis with a 90-day investment score based on probability of gain, so you're not wasting time coding a bot for a stock that's fundamentally weak. Once you have a solid pick, then you can use Claude to code the backtest with realistic cost assumptions—but don't skip the stock analysis layer.
